content: A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI. How does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious? Scientists have spent decades studying how neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals, yet the physical processes that allow us to recall experiences, attach feelings to them, and give them meaning remain incompletely understood. A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells. Rather than viewing memory primarily as a product of neuronal activity, the researchers propose that interactions among neurons, supporting brain cells, and molecules in their surrounding environment could play a fundamental role in shaping thought and conscious experience. Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Prof. Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Department of Chemistry present their theory in Consciousness, Memory, and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective . Building on earlier research into how experiences might be physically stored in the brain, they examine whether the chemistry of memory could help explain the origins of thought and consciousness. Their proposal also raises a question about artificial intelligence: If human memory and emotion depend on the chemistry of living cells, can computers ever develop consciousness simply by becoming more powerful? Scientists have long studied how neurons communicate to form and retrieve memories. But Marx and Gilon suggest that important parts of this process may also occur in the molecular environment surrounding brain cells. Their model, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, involves three interacting components: brain cells, particularly neurons and astrocytes; the molecular material surrounding those cells; and chemicals such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters. According to the theory, these components could allow the brain to chemically encode and retrieve information. Rather than serving only as a support structure, the environment surrounding brain cells may actively participate in memory storage. Astrocytes, star-shaped cells that interact closely with neurons, play a central role in the proposed mechanism. The researchers suggest that coordinated activity among these cells, neurons, and surrounding molecules could contribute to how memories are formed and processed. A familiar song can bring back memories from decades ago, complete with feelings that seemed long forgotten. Such experiences show that remembering involves more than retrieving information. Marx and Gilon propose that the emotional content of memories may be linked to their chemical encoding. In their model, signaling molecules, including neurotransmitters and gliotransmitters, help connect stored information with the feelings associated with an experience. The researchers also suggest that retrieving and interpreting these chemically stored memories may contribute to the emergence of thought. In this view, memory is not simply a record of past events but an active process through which the brain assigns meaning to experience. Computers and brains both store and process information, but the underlying mechanisms differ. While computers rely on electronic hardware, biological memory involves living cells and complex chemical interactions. Marx and Gilon argue that this distinction could matter for consciousness. AI systems can perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks, but their ability to process information does not establish that they experience thoughts or emotions. For example, an AI system can identify a familiar song and describe the memories or feelings it might evoke in a person. Whether such a system could actually experience nostalgia is a different question. The researchers suggest that if consciousness depends partly on the biochemical processes involved in human memory, greater computational power alone may not be sufficient to reproduce it. The proposed model offers a possible connection between memory, emotion, and thought, but it does not establish how physical processes in the brain produce conscious experience. The authors acknowledge that consciousness remains poorly understood and do not claim to have demonstrated that AI cannot become conscious. Instead, their work suggests that investigating the chemical mechanisms of memory could help explain how stored experiences acquire emotional meaning and contribute to thought. Whether those processes are essential for consciousness remains an open question. Reference: “Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective” by Gerard Marx and Chaim Gilon, 4 August 2026, International Journal of Psychiatry Research . title: Palo Alto inks $4.5 billion deal for AI startup Applied Compute, shares pop 7% on earnings
content: Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates and inked a deal for artificial intelligence startup Applied Compute . Here's how the company did versus LSEG estimates: Revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter. Fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. Amid this backdrop, the company's shares have jumped 85% this year. "As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely," CEO Nikesh Arora said in a release. Palo Alto said annual recurring revenue for its next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history. The cybersecurity company bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027 as businesses spend more on security in the age of AI. Palo Alto expects adjusted earnings per share in the range of $4.26 to $4.30 and revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion. The forecasts topped the earnings of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue expected by analysts. Net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share, a year ago. Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI. Arora said the company's $4.5 billion all-stock deal for Applied Compute will help businesses secure open-weight models as adoption grows. The startup helps businesses run and customize their own AI models and marks a major investment for Palo Alto beyond cybersecurity. "If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on an earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do." Outages from Microsoft, banks and air traffic control have heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week. U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity, but experts say the rapid acceleration in patching is straining dated systems. As businesses discover more vulnerabilities, Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year. "Whatever they do today is going to take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is," Arora said.

title: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
content: An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO . Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm. Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab. Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way. Anthropic's earliest backers connected with the company through philanthropic circles worried about AI's existential risk. They're sometimes described as "doomers." In 2020, Tallinn told CNBC that there's a 1-in-6 chance that humans won't survive this century, referencing a book from Oxford professor Toby Ord. Tallinn also described a runaway AI scenario where a model is left working overnight and "the world is no longer there in the morning." While he continued to work in tech, Tallinn co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute , known for one of the first public calls to pause AI. Despite high-profile signatories , including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the institute's "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter in 2023 had little effect on the industry. Tallinn's view on AI was influenced by researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who co-authored the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies," about the catastrophic risk of AI without proper checks, according to a person familiar with the matter. Tallinn, who has an estimated net worth of more than $10 billion, later crossed paths with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had defected from OpenAI with his eventual co-founders, citing views that Sam Altman's company wasn't taking AI safety seriously enough. Amodei and Tallinn overlapped in the effective altruism community, according to people who know both of them. Effective altruism, sometimes known as EA , is a philosophy that aims to use data and evidence to maximize philanthropic impact. While there's no official membership, its Silicon Valley network ended up generating much of Anthropic's early venture capital money, according to multiple people. Tallinn's early bet was that bankrolling a safety-conscious AI company was one of the best ways to keep a lid on the risk, these people said. Tallinn also invested in DeepMind, which was later acquired by Google . One person, who asked not to be named, said that at the time of Tallinn's investment, there was no expectation that Anthropic "would be a profitable undertaking." Venture investors hadn't yet gone all-in on AI, and it was "before the era of putting AI in your pitch deck," said the person, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the matter. Tallinn declined to be interviewed for this story. Anthropic's first round in 2021 also included Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, who founded Open Philanthropy — now known as Coefficient Giving — which is deeply rooted in effective altruism. The charity was co-founded by Holden Karnofsky, husband of Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Karnofsky also started GiveWell, also largely tied to effective altruism. Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, another known effective altruist, backed Anthropic in its early days alongside Tallinn. Bankman-Fried participated in the Series B in 2022 through his now-defunct hedge fund Alameda Research. The former CEO was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His stake was sold in bankruptcy auction at a fraction of the company's current valuation. Tallinn's early investment initially put Anthropic's price tag at $461 million, according to Pitchbook. It has ballooned in value since, and last raised money at a $965 billion valuation in private markets. The lab has raised money from tech giants Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia, and plans to sell $26 billion worth of shares to a group of tech companies at the IPO price. Anthropic's early investors and some in the safety community aren't overwhelmingly cheering the IPO. Many worry behind the scenes that AI safety will take a back seat to Anthropic's commercial success and wider shareholder base, according to a person close to the group. Many in the AI safety community "are opposed to the IPO," this person said. Others point to Anthropic's unique corporate structure that gives the founders broad discretion and control of the company through a single super-voting share. The co-founders will be sole members of "Founder LLC," which will hold 50.1% of the voting power. But Anthropic is also built as a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a dual mandate beyond just a duty to shareholders. It has to serve the best interests of its "company purpose" to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
